desc:
The digital root of a positive integer is found by repeatedly replacing it with the sum of its decimal digits until a single digit remains. For example, 38 becomes 11 and then 2, so its digital root is 2.

Each query is a pair [l, r]. For each query, compute the sum of the digital roots of all integers from l to r inclusive, and return that sum modulo 1000000007. Return the answers in query order.

queries = [[1, 9], [10, 18], [1, 20]] -> [45, 45, 93]
queries = [[5, 5]]                    -> [5]
hints: Summing digital roots one at a time is too slow when the ranges reach 109. Define a prefix function S(n) that gives the sum for 1..n, and answer each query as a difference.
Nine consecutive integers have digital roots 1 through 9, one each, so every full block of nine contributes 45.
The leftover m = n % 9 numbers at the end of 1..n have digital roots 1, 2, ..., m, which add up to m * (m + 1) / 2.
editorial: For positive x the digital root is 1 + (x - 1) % 9. So the digital roots repeat with period 9, with values 1 through 9 in each period. Define S(n) = 45 * (n // 9) + m * (m + 1) / 2 with m = n % 9, which is the sum over 1..n.

Each query is S(r) - S(l - 1), reduced modulo 1000000007. The Python integers are exact, so the subtraction cannot overflow, and the modulo keeps the result inside 32 bits. Every query takes constant time.
